value.overview: The White-crowned Pigeon (Patagioenas leucocephala) is a large, dark Caribbean pigeon recognized by its contrasting white crown, pale eyes, pinkish bill, and pink legs. It spends much of its time in forest canopies, where it feeds mainly on fruits. The species is strongly associated with coastal and island habitats, especially mangroves and lowland forests. Although widespread in the Caribbean, it is extremely rare in Costa Rica and is best regarded there as an accidental or casual visitor.
value.classification: The White-crowned Pigeon belongs to the pigeon and dove family Columbidae and the order Columbiformes. It is a New World pigeon in the genus Patagioenas.
value.identification: Adults are large pigeons with mostly slate-gray to dark gray plumage, a conspicuous white crown, pale or white eyes, and a pinkish bill with a paler tip. The nape may show greenish iridescence in good light. Females generally have a duller, grayer crown and slightly browner tones. Immatures are browner overall and usually show only a weakly developed pale crown. In flight, the species appears dark-bodied and broad-winged, often traveling high above coastal habitats.
value.rangeHabitat: The species is distributed mainly across the Caribbean, including the Bahamas, Cuba, Jamaica, Hispaniola, Puerto Rico, the Cayman Islands, the Florida Keys, and parts of the Caribbean coast of Central America. It uses mangrove islands, coastal woodland, lowland forest, forest edges, and other areas with fruiting trees, sometimes traveling inland to feed. In Costa Rica it is not a regular resident or breeder; reliable national references describe it as casual or accidental along the Caribbean coast. The Tortuguero–Barra del Colorado area and the Sixaola region are considered the most plausible areas for occasional occurrence.
value.migrationStatus: Generally resident or locally dispersive within the Caribbean, with regular movements between island roosting or nesting sites and mainland fruiting forests. In Costa Rica it is an extremely rare, irregular visitor rather than a regular migrant; its occurrence is likely linked to movements from nearby Caribbean breeding areas.
value.breeding: White-crowned Pigeons commonly breed in coastal mangroves, small wooded islands, and lowland forests, sometimes in loose colonies. The nest is a flimsy platform of sticks placed in trees or shrubs, often above water or in dense vegetation. Usually one or two eggs are laid, and both adults participate in incubation and care of the young. Breeding information from Costa Rica is lacking, and the species is not considered an established breeding bird there.
value.dietFeeding: Fruit is the principal food, including fruits of figs and other tropical trees, with seeds and small amounts of other plant material also taken. The pigeon usually forages in tree crowns and may travel considerable distances between mangrove roosting sites and inland or mainland trees bearing ripe fruit. It often feeds quietly in dense foliage, making it easier to detect by its flight calls or movement than by direct observation.
value.behavior: White-crowned Pigeons are often shy and may be seen alone, in pairs, or in small flocks. They are powerful fliers and regularly make long daily flights over open water between roosting, nesting, and feeding areas. Birds may perch unobtrusively in forest canopies and give slow, repetitive cooing calls. In Costa Rica, any individual should be treated as an unusual record requiring careful documentation because the species is not regularly encountered.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is considered to be declining, although exact population estimates and trends vary among regions.
conservation.threats: Important concerns include the loss and degradation of mangrove, coastal, and lowland forest habitat; development of Caribbean islands and shorelines; hunting in parts of the range; and disturbance or predation at nesting colonies. Dependence on intact fruiting forests and small coastal islands can make local populations vulnerable to habitat change.
conservation.howToHelp: Protect mangroves, coastal woodland, lowland forest, and fruiting trees throughout the species’ range. Support conservation of Caribbean islands and coastal wetlands, discourage hunting, and avoid disturbing nesting or roosting colonies. In Costa Rica, observers should document unusual records carefully and report them to local bird-record committees or conservation organizations, helping improve knowledge of this rare visitor.
